overview: Two types of operons distinguished by their default state and what kind of molecule flips that state.
genZNote: Inducible operon: normally off, needs a substrate to switch it on. Repressible operon: normally on, needs a product to shut it off.

aspects.label: Default State
aspects.valueA: Normally switched OFF; turned ON by an inducer molecule.
aspects.valueB: Normally switched ON; turned OFF by a corepressor molecule.

aspects.label: Typical Metabolic Context
aspects.valueA: Common in catabolic pathways, where the substrate itself induces the enzymes needed to break it down.
aspects.valueB: Common in anabolic (biosynthetic) pathways, where the end product represses further synthesis.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: The lac operon, induced by lactose.
aspects.valueB: The trp operon, repressed by tryptophan when it's already abundant.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: The lac operon (inducible, catabolic) and trp operon (repressible, anabolic) are the two textbook examples almost always paired together in exam questions.
overlay.memoryTrick: Inducible = OFF by default, substrate switches it ON. Repressible = ON by default, product switches it OFF.
overlay.commonMisconception: 'Repressible' doesn't mean the operon is normally off like an inducible one — it's actually the opposite, since a repressible operon starts out active and gets shut down only when its product builds up.
